text: Research question, be rigorous and concise. What EXACTLY distinguishes the Monty Hall paradox from ordinary Bayesian updating? Propose necessary-and-sufficient structural conditions (a formal definition of a 'Monty effect') stated in terms of the likelihoods P(observation | hypothesis, my action). Candidates to test: (i) the observation is generated by an agent who knows the hidden state (protocol dependence); (ii) the revealer is constrained by MY choice (my option is protected); (iii) the same observation has different likelihoods under hypotheses that were symmetric a priori; (iv) the protected option's probability is conserved (martingale) while mass flows to the unprotected survivor; (v) my own action is a parent of the evidence, making the evidence a collider of (my pick, prize). For each condition give a counterexample showing it is NOT sufficient, or a proof that it is. End with a one-line definition and a numeric 'Monty index' that is 0 for plain Bayes (e.g. base-rate problems, Monty Fall) and positive for Monty Hall, computed for 4 variants.
